The Huffington Post has piece up titled "Conservative Majority In Senate Could Give Trudeau Trouble" highlights two problems with partisan politics

  1. the publication is looking to create a partisan reaction to a problem that doesn't exist. The Conservative Party of Canada holds 47 seats in the Senate under the control of whoever they choose as their new party leader. There are 36 other Senators and 22 vacant seats that are unlikely to remain vacant for very long; 36 + 22 = 58, and since 58 is greater than 47 there is no problem.

  2. an anonymous Conservative Senator says

"We're going to deal with them just like they dealt with us when they were the majority," said one senior Conservative senator, who spoke on condition of anonymity because the caucus had yet to discuss its next steps.

Most negotiations, the senator said, will be civil, although Conservatives may not freely give their votes on legislation.

"I don't have any responsibility to pass Liberal legislation."

....... and there is the problem.

It is the job of Senators to review legislation sent to them from the House of Commons and determine if there are any issues that need to be addressed based on why the Senate was created.

The Senate was created to counterbalance representation by population in the House of Commons. In recent years, the Senate has come to bolster representation of groups often underrepresented in Parliament, such as Aboriginal peoples, visible minorities and women. The Senate was also intended to provide Parliament with a second chance to consider bills before they are passed.

Party considerations are not mentioned.

The Conservative Senator who wishes to remain anonymous is right, s/he is under no obligation to pass Liberal legislation; but regardless of what certain political parties and their leaders may believe the job of a Senator is not to follow the orders of their party leader like good little drones. A Senators obligation is to review legislation in a non-partisan manner and, if it is not found to be illegal, and/or lacking, and/or detrimental to the country and/or the region they are tasked with representing, their job is to pass it.

To return to what the petulant and anonymous Conservative Party Senator said regarding how they were treated under previous Liberal governments s/he should be reminded that things are not like they were when their party sat in Opposition in The House. There is no longer a Liberal Party Caucus in the Senate that takes their marching orders from the PMO, there is probably a caucus of Liberal Senators who were appointed by former Liberal Prime Ministers - but they are not part of a larger "Liberal" parliamentary caucus and, to repeat, no longer take their marching orders from the PMO.

Conservative Senators, the Conservative Party of Canada, and whoever its interim and eventual next leader may be, can look at the new order and govern themselves accordingly, or they can continue to operate under archaic practices and, like their former leader who recently resigned in defeat, ignore the new order and find themselves irrelevant and remembered primarily for their failure to see that Canada changed, but they were unable to and ultimately found lacking.
Defined: The Problem With Partisan Politics

I know the Senate is usually a rubber stamp, but that's because it is usually controlled by the government in the HoC. The Senate has to be functional, or else it has to be shut down. It can't be in between. I don't believe it should be shut down, but it should be cleaned up. I would have no problem with non-partisan, independent senators chosen by a panel. I would also not have a problem with putting the Senate back to the way it was before Harper stopped appointing new ones, after they clean up their spending issues and finish kicking out senators who were abusing their expense accounts.

I fail to see how the Senate would be rendered dysfunctional.

He has to pack the Senate with Liberals so he can implement his agenda.

That's old school partisan thinking that not only presupposes that the only way legislation can make it through the Senate is by being whipped, but runs contrary to why the Senate was created. The Senate exists as a balance to the short term partisan interests of the House which suffer from the 'will of the majority party in The House' syndrome. Although they call themselves a majority government the vast majority of majority governments are in power as a result of the decisions of the greatest minority of voters - Trudeau's government is no exception - and the Senate is supposed to take a longer less partisan view than the next election and satisfying a political base that represents a fraction of the whole. Since the time of at least Trudeau the first the Senate has become more and more partisan and faltered considerably in its duty, more so in the last 8 or 9 years than previously, that does not mean that the ship has acquired such a list cannot be righted.

The senators do not know whether Trudeau will exercise his prerogative to name a new speaker for the Senate or what exactly Trudeau will do about the 22 vacancies in the Senate left behind by outgoing Conservative Prime Minister Stephen Harper.

Trudeau may, or may not, exercise his prerogative to name a Senate Speaker - or he may decide that, as in The House, the Speaker is chosen by the Senate itself. I would presume that would take place after the 22 vacancies have been filled so the process is not as tainted by partisan considerations..

With respect to Senators not knowing what Trudeau will do with those vacancies - that's BS. The promise was to create a non-partisan committee to make recommendations to the PM regarding appointing Senators, I know that, you know that, and anyone who followed this election knows that. If Trudeau fails, within a reasonable time frame, to follow through on that commitment then we may have an issue.

The Senate has to be functional, or else it has to be shut down.

The Senate has not been a functional part of Canadian democracy for years - it has become a simple and expensive extension of the will of the party leader in power and little else. Their spending issues are IMO, the least of their problems when compared to their hyper-partisan problems.

Silhouetted Samurai Slasher Dawn Of The Ronin Gets A Demo

5 Minute Impressions:

  • Really satisfying combat that has depth through simplicity. There only seem to be a few attacks, but it is really satisfying to cut through a horde of enemies. It says there'll be more attacks, but I'm happy with what's there thus far.

  • I absolutely love the art style. Silhouette style has always been a particular favorite of mine. I thought that the silhouette levels in DKC: Tropical freeze were some of the best looking things I've seen in any game in a long time and am happy to see a game embracing it in full.

  • The requirements are rather high; I managed around 15 FPS on High with no video card, 30 FPS on Low with no video card (Intel 3000 series with an older laptop i7 backing it), and 60 FPS (with some dips when there are a lot of enemies) on low with the video card (7700M). I didn't see much of a difference between High and Low though, and your mileage may vary. In other words, it's deceptively demanding. It probably will be further optimized upon release, so there's that.

  • It is an early release: the menus are clunky to navigate, weird shit happens, and I can't get past the first story cutscene due to crashing (all of my impressions are from the dojo mode). If it's like this on release, it'll suck, but I can forgive an early beta demo, especially with what is there being so impressive.

I went from not knowing that this game exists to really looking forward to it in less than 15 minutes, which is awesome.
